title: Assessing the influence of repeated exposures and mental stress on human wayfinding performance in indoor environments using virtual reality technology
authors: Jing Lin, Lijun Cao, Nan Li, 2019
research_question: First, how do repeated exposures influence human wayfinding performance in exploring and egressing from indoor environments? Second, how does mental stress in fire evacuation interact with repeated exposures to influence human wayfinding performance during indoor fire emergency evacuation?

participants.description: 20.9 ± 1.96 years old on average, ranging from 18 to 25; 24 males and 24 females; Chinese undergraduate and graduate students from a major university in Beijing, China. All had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no color blindness.
participants.recruitment: Distributed a call-for-participant flyer through online social media. Participants were invited on a first-come, first-served basis.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: An immersive virtual museum (38m L x 15m W x 3m H) developed using Unity3D and presented via HTC VIVE HMD. Virtual fire (4.2m x 6.6m) and smoke (38m x 15m, up to 3m high) were simulated at specific locations during egress tasks in fire emergency conditions. Standard fire alarm sounds were also included.

mechanisms: Reduced visibility and mental stress during fire emergency adversely impact wayfinding performance by affecting landmark recognition, position assessment, and promoting random route choices.
Repeated exposure enhances wayfinding performance by improving landmark knowledge and procedural knowledge, which are less susceptible to environmental visibility and mental stress.

Spatial knowledge acquired through prior experience and stored in the cognitive map can endure partial loss over time, suggesting that repeated exposures separated by time intervals may have different effects.
A potential threshold of repeated exposures (one or two) exists, beyond which spatial memories and wayfinding performance may not further improve.
implementation_implications: Building design optimization (e.g., circulation in commercial buildings).
Support for building fire emergency management in practice.

limitations: Participants were university students, limiting external validity to elders, children, or people with different cultural backgrounds.

The degree of reality experienced by participants in the IVE could be further enhanced by introducing additional human senses and dynamic scenarios (e.g., real walking, smelling fire, dynamic obstacles, human group interaction).

The threshold of repeated exposures (one or two) was observed under a particular time interval of two weeks; whether this threshold changes or exists with different time intervals requires further investigation.
